division.heading: Request for Particulars, Amendments to Pleadings and Close of Pleadings

operative_text.controlling:
3.63(1)  Unless the Court otherwise orders, if a party amends a
pleading, a new pleading must be filed, being a copy of the original
pleading as amended.
(2)  The amendment must
(a) be dated and identified, and each amended version must
be identified, and
(b) be endorsed by the court clerk in the following form:
Amended on [date] by [order] [party consent]
Dated . . .

BOOK_C.title: Identifying amendments to pleadings
BOOK_C.division_heading: Division 4 – REQUEST FOR PARTICULARS, AMENDMENTS TO PLEADINGS AND CLOSE OF PLEADINGS

commentary.text: There is no specific rule or authority governing the identification of amendments in pleadings. It was once common to use underlining (red for the first amendment, then green, and various other colours for subsequent amendments). The most common contemporary practice, acceptable to the clerks, is single underlining for first amendments, double underlining for second amendments and dotted-line underlining for third amendments, with no need to use different colours, or any particular colours, though colours are often used in conjunction with this practice.
